```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)

# Must match EXPERIMENT.id in experiment.js, and the --experiment you passed to the export.
# Phase 1 moves feng2024-pilot-a -> feng2024-pilot-b -> feng2024-final; change it here each time.

experiment_id        <- "feng2024-lite-final"

```

```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures.
#
# Feng & Rutledge (2024), Experiment 2, n = 200 (Results, p. 3; Fig. 2A):
# rare minus common risk taking = 4.03 +/- 1.06 % (mean +/- SEM), p < .001 (Wilcoxon).
original_n    <- 200
original_mean <- 4.03
original_sem  <- 1.06
original_sd   <- original_sem * sqrt(original_n)   # about 15.0 percentage points
original_dz   <- original_mean / original_sd       # about 0.27
# The paper reports no CI; this one is computed from the mean and SEM.
orig_ci       <- original_mean + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, original_n - 1) * original_sem

# Risk-taking rates by sequence type, for the side-by-side figure. Not printed in the paper;
# computed from the authors' Experiment 2 data (OSF, data_csv/Exp2_data_taskdata.csv), which
# reproduce the paper's 4.03 +/- 1.06 exactly.
original_rates <- tibble(
  sequence = c("Common", "Rare"),
  mean     = c(46.53, 50.57),   # % risky choices, mean across participants
  sem      = c(1.05, 1.17),
  n        = original_n
)
# Secondary effect (perseveration): stay rate, rare minus common = -3.62 +/- 0.89 % (p. 4).
original_stay_mean <- -3.62
original_stay_sem  <- 0.89
```

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"
# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 1e5)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  # Sessions run by the automated test robot (?fast=1, only possible on localhost) are not data.
  if ("fast_mode" %in% names(participants)) participants <- participants |> filter(!(fast_mode %in% TRUE))
  if (!"headphone_passed" %in% names(participants)) participants$headphone_passed <- NA

  complete <- participants |> filter(completed %in% TRUE)

  # Exclusion rule: replace with the rule you preregister. Here: passed the headphone check
  # (5 or more of 6 correct; failing ends the study) and has all 120 choice trials.
  n_choice <- trials |> filter(task == "choice") |> count(participant_id, name = "n_choice")
  checked <- complete |>
    left_join(n_choice, by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(n_choice = coalesce(n_choice, 0L))
  keep <- checked |> filter(headphone_passed %in% TRUE, n_choice == 120)

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, keep = keep,
       n_headphone_fail = sum(participants$headphone_passed %in% FALSE),
       n_missing_trials = sum(checked$headphone_passed %in% TRUE & checked$n_choice < 120))
}

# Per-participant percentages of risky choices (and of staying with the previous choice)
# after common and rare sequences, and the rare-minus-common differences.
person_effects <- function(d) {
  d$trials |>
    filter(task == "choice", participant_id %in% d$keep$participant_id) |>
    mutate(rare = as.logical(rare), chose_risky = as.numeric(chose_risky), stay = as.numeric(stay)) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(risky_rare   = 100 * mean(chose_risky[rare]),
              risky_common = 100 * mean(chose_risky[!rare]),
              stay_rare    = 100 * mean(stay[rare], na.rm = TRUE),
              stay_common  = 100 * mean(stay[!rare], na.rm = TRUE),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(risk_diff = risky_rare - risky_common, stay_diff = stay_rare - stay_common)
}

# The key statistic: mean rare-minus-common difference with SEM and 95% CI, d_z, and the
# two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against zero (the original's test). NULL with < 2 people.
effect_summary <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  n <- length(x)
  if (n < 2) return(NULL)
  m <- mean(x); s <- sd(x); sem <- s / sqrt(n)
  w <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided", exact = FALSE)),
                error = function(e) list(statistic = NA_real_, p.value = NA_real_))
  tibble(N = n, estimate = m, sem = sem,
         ci_low = m - qt(0.975, n - 1) * sem, ci_high = m + qt(0.975, n - 1) * sem,
         dz = if (s > 0) m / s else NA_real_,
         V = unname(w$statistic), p = w$p.value)
}

# Mean % risky after common and rare sequences, for the side-by-side figure.
sequence_rates <- function(pe) {
  pe |>
    pivot_longer(c(risky_common, risky_rare), names_to = "sequence", values_to = "pct") |>
    mutate(sequence = if_else(sequence == "risky_rare", "Rare", "Common")) |>
    group_by(sequence) |>
    summarise(mean = mean(pct), sem = sd(pct) / sqrt(n()), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
}

# Side-by-side figure: any number of studies on the same axes, in the order given. Points are
# means, error bars 95% CIs, and a line joins each study's common and rare rates.
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           half = qt(0.975, pmax(n - 1, 1)) * sem,
           label = sprintf("n = %d", n))
  cols <- setNames(c("grey45", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.35)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = sequence, y = mean, colour = Study, group = Study)) +
    geom_line(position = dodge, linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - half, ymax = mean + half), position = dodge, width = 0.12) +
    geom_point(position = dodge, size = 3) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = cols) +
    labs(x = "Tone sequence before the choice", y = "Chose the risky option (%)", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

# Formatting helpers shared by the tables.
fmt_p <- function(p) if (is.na(p)) "" else format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
key_row <- function(study, r = NULL, p_text = NULL) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Effect (rare − common)` = "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", d_z = "", `Wilcoxon p` = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Effect (rare − common)` = sprintf("%.2f points", r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         d_z = sprintf("%.2f", r$dz),
         `Wilcoxon p` = p_text %||% fmt_p(r$p))
}
original_effect <- tibble(N = original_n, estimate = original_mean, ci_low = orig_ci[1],
                          ci_high = orig_ci[2], dz = original_dz, p = NA_real_)
p1_effect <- if (have_data) effect_summary(person_effects(phase1)$risk_diff)
p2_effect <- if (have_phase2) effect_summary(person_effects(phase2)$risk_diff)

bind_rows(
  key_row("Original (Experiment 2)", original_effect, p_text = "< .001"),
  key_row("Phase 1: replication", p1_effect),
  key_row("Phase 2: extension", p2_effect)
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrlllr",
    caption = "Key comparison: percentage of risky choices after rare minus common tone sequences, per participant (original CI computed from its mean and SEM).")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction
I’m interested in applying mathematical modelling technique to model psychological process. Coming from mathematical finance background, the Feng & Rutledge (2024)’s research on surprising sounds influence risky decision making fit my interest and bridge the gap between psychology, behavioural finance, and mathematical modelling. This paper also highlighted how external stimuli like surprising sounds can influence one’s attitude towards risk taking, which also has been studied in professional traders (e.g. trading floor buzzer or surprising news announcement in trading floor) and casino floor.

For the specific experiment that I replicated, experiment 2, each participant can decide whether they want to choose a ‘safe’ or ‘risky’ option in every trial, with the aim of maximising their cumulative wealth. Each participant start with 500 points and the outcome of risky option is revealed after 1.3 seconds delay if chosen. In total, there were 120 trials and the participants received fixed monetary reward irrespective of their final outcome. For the stimulus, each participant is presented with 6-tone auditory sequence, with 3 different frequencies, i.e. A=1000 Hz, B=1500 Hz, and C=500 Hz. In 75% of the trials participants hear ‘common sequence’ : AAAAAA, and for the remaining 25% of the trials participants hear ‘rare sequence’: AAAAAB or AAAAAC. Experimenter alternate the location of risky choice from left to right (or right to left) of the screen for every 10 trials. To run this experiment, we recruited participants in Prolific with the following criteria: age 18+ and fluent in English, no hearing difficulty, have access to laptop, and earphone. We aimed to recruit 120 participants in total and we built the experiment in jspsych. 

There were several challenges that we anticipated in running this experiment, including limited budget to recruit participants in-time, participants attention and audio quality are hard to control, moving from Gorilla (original experiment platform) to jsPsych with firebase. 
For the **key statistical test**, we calculated the percentage difference of each participant’s risky choices in rare trial and in common trial and perform the 2-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test (against 0), to be consistent with the authors.

One possible extension to this experiment is incorporating ‘think like a trader’ reframing (Sokol-Hessner et al. 2009) to half of the participants (randomly, N=100) to test if it reduces loss aversion and effect of surprising sounds.

## Methods

### Power analysis


The original effect size is 4.03 ± 1.6% (i.e. % points of risky choice for rare minus common tone sequence), d_z = 0.27 with N = 200 participants. As we can see from the power table below, we need 116 participants (Wilcoxon) for 80 % power, 155 for 90%, and 191 for 95%. The other alternative that one could use is 2.5 times the original sample size (500 participants), as published effect tend to be inflated. We choose to power the study to the original effect and aim for the minimum sample size of interest to achieve at least 80 \% power, which led us to choose N=120 participants. Budget constraint was also part of our consideration, which limit the number of participants we could recruit. 

```{r}
#| label: power
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n_t <- power.t.test(delta = original_mean, sd = original_sd, power = pw,
                      sig.level = 0.05, type = "one.sample")$n
  tibble(Power = scales::percent(pw), `N (t-test)` = ceiling(n_t),
         `N (Wilcoxon, ~5% more)` = ceiling(n_t / 0.955))
})
knitr::kable(power_rows, caption = sprintf(
  "Sample needed to detect the original effect (%.2f%% rare minus common, d_z = %.2f), two-sided alpha = .05.",
  original_mean, original_dz))
two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original_n)
```

For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample would be `r two_and_half`.

### Planned sample


We recruited from Prolific, with the following criterias: Age 18+, fluent in English, reside in the US, have access to desktop or laptop with keyboard and headphone or earphone. We collected the data until N=120 participants passed the exclusion criteria. 
Based on Pilot A (N=3), participants spent 15 to 20 minutes to complete the task, so we compensated participants for 17 minutes of their time. This is further confirmed by Pilot B data (N=6), with participants median time of 17 minutes.


### Materials

We followed the set-up of Experiment 2 in the original paper:
For the tones sequence, we used 6 of 100 ms pure tones in each sequence, each 400 ms apart. Each tone has frequencies of A/B/C = 1000/1500/500 Hz, with the split of 75% common and 25% rare sequence of tones. 
For the gamble amounts, based on authors' Experiment 2 data, we incorporated 40 trials per type with sure loss of −25.
For the soundcheck, we modified this slightly to 2 screens headphone check with replay (instead of 6) and we required participants to get both check right before proceeding with the experiment. This was done for the interest of time and to enhance participants experience.
The live experiment is available at the link above for reference. <https://psych251.github.io/feng2024/lite/> 

### Procedure

For the experiment sequence and trials design, we followed closely the original Experiment 2 set-up, but for interest of time and to enhance participants experience we dropped the PHQ-8 questionnaires at the end of the experiment. Upon opening the experiment page, each participant started with consent form (agree / disagree to participate), followed by welcome page, volume calibration, and sound check. After passing the sound check, participants were directed to the practice round for familiarization and sequence checks, followed by instructions for the main task and the main task of 120 trials. After finishing the main task, participants were directed to another tone sequence checks, followed by demographics page with optional comments, and debrief.

Each trial has the following timing: 3s fixation, 1.3s gamble delay, 1s outcome, and 2s safe outcome. Just as in the original experiment, we swapped the risky option’s side from left to right (or right to left) every 10 trials.

Based on Pilot A data, each participant took around 15 to 20 minutes to finish the whole experiment (from loading the page to debrief). This is further confirmed by Pilot B data.
We refer interested reader to our live experiment page above for reference.


### Pilot Testing: 

#### Pilot A: 
In Pilot A, we ran the experiment with N=3 participants to check every variables are logged correctly. The completion time for each participant was between 15 to 20 minutes.

#### Pilot B: 
In Pilot B, we ran the experiment in Prolific with N=6 participants (who completed the task). 
In terms of dropout, 13 participants started the experiment: 2 turned down by device check, 3 failed sound check, 1 stopped before starting the task, and 6 successfully completed the task.
In terms of comprehension, all 6 participants who successfully completed the experiment passed sound check and sequence check before and after the task.
The median time taken to complete the task was 17 minutes.
No changes were made after Pilot A and B.




### Analysis plan



**Key analysis of interest.** 

We are interested in the difference between the percentage of risky choices chosen by each participant following rare and common tone sequence (% risky choice with rare - % risky choice with common ), we tested this using 2-sided Wilcoxon rank test against 0.




**Exclusions.** 
We excluded participants who failed the headphone (sound) check or didn't complete the study.



### Differences from the original study


| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | Adults recruited on Prolific (18+, fluent in English)| Adults recruited on Prolific  (18+, fluent in English, based in US ) | No. |
| Platform | Gorilla | JsPsych | No. |
| Headphone Check |6 trials played once  (min. 5 correct to pass), | 2 trials with replay allowed (2/2 correct to pass) | Unlikely, participants who didn't use headphone failed the headphone-check despite allowing replay |
|Sample size | 200  | 120 | Unlikely, with N=120 the power is 80% at the original effect (acceptable level)|
| Other tasks | PHQ-8 / GAD Questionnaires Included  | PHQ-8 / GAD Questionnaires Removed | No. |

### Methods addendum (post data collection)


#### Actual sample

From 297 participants who started the experiment, 277 passed the device check, and 142 passed the sound check. 122 of those finished the experiments, but 2 timed-out and excluded. We analysed results from 120 participants who passed the device check, sound check, and finished the experiments (without timed-out). The average participants age is 40.3 years, with 62 men and 58 women. The median time to complete the experiment is 18.7 minutes (against 17 mins that we compensated based on the pilot result).

## Results

### Data preparation

No data processing beyond applying the pre-registered exclusion rule (sound check and completing 120 trials).
We reported the key-statistics and report and how they were calculated in the confirmatory analysis section.

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Key test: per participant, % risky choices after rare minus after common sequences;
# two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against zero, as in the original.
if (nrow(pe) >= 2) {
  print(suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(pe$risk_diff, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided", exact = FALSE)))
  effect_summary(pe$risk_diff) |>
    transmute(N, `Mean (points)` = round(estimate, 2), SEM = round(sem, 2),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high), d_z = round(dz, 2),
              V, p = fmt_p(p)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Key test: rare minus common risky choices, per participant.")
} else {
  message("Key test not run: it needs at least 2 analysed participants; there are ", nrow(pe), ".")
}
```

We did two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against 0, for the percentage difference of risky choices after rare and common tone. As shown in the table, with N=120, we get +2.14 mean difference (estimate), 1.35 SEM,  95% confidence interval of [−0.53, 4.81], effect size d_z = mean difference / std. dev of difference =  0.14, and p-value = 0.36. 
Compare to the original studies of mean difference +4.03, 95% CI of [1.94, 6.12], p < .001, and d_z = 0.27.



### Replication assessment


The confidence interval of our replication result includes both 0 and also the original estimate of +4.03, hence we can say our result is inconclusive. 
The calculated effect size d_z = 0.14 is only half of the original effect size d_z = 0.27. 



```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
rep <- effect_summary(pe$risk_diff)

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(
    tibble(Study = "Original (Experiment 2)", N = original_n, estimate = original_mean,
           ci_low = orig_ci[1], ci_high = orig_ci[2], p_text = "< .001"),
    rep |> transmute(Study = "Phase 1: replication", N, estimate, ci_low, ci_high, p_text = fmt_p(p))
  ) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Difference (rare − common)` = sprintf("%.2f points", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              `Wilcoxon p` = p_text) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: rare minus common percentage of risky choices.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least 2 analysed participants.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- original_mean >= rep$ci_low & original_mean <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.2f points. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    original_mean))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

### Exploratory analyses

We analysed replay users vs non-replay users after collecting our data and stay rate: rate of people making the same choice as on the previous trial. The results are reported in the table below. 
B
```{r}
#| label: exploratory-replay
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory (not preregistered): the rare-tone effect for participants who did and did not use
# Replay in the 2-screen headphone check. Within each group: two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test
# against zero; between groups: two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney) test.
replay_use <- trials |>
  filter(task == "headphone_check", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  summarise(used_replay = sum(as.numeric(replays), na.rm = TRUE) > 0, .groups = "drop")
pe_replay <- pe |> left_join(replay_use, by = "participant_id")
by_replay <- pe_replay |>
  group_by(Group = if_else(used_replay %in% TRUE, "Used Replay", "No Replay")) |>
  group_modify(~ effect_summary(.x$risk_diff)) |>
  ungroup()
by_replay |>
  transmute(Group, N, `Mean (points)` = round(estimate, 2), SEM = round(sem, 2),
            `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high), p = map_chr(p, fmt_p)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: rare minus common risky choices by Replay use in the headphone check (Wilcoxon signed-rank test against zero within each group).")
rs <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(risk_diff ~ used_replay, data = pe_replay, exact = FALSE))
message(sprintf("Between groups (Wilcoxon rank-sum): W = %.1f, p = %s", rs$statistic, fmt_p(rs$p.value)))
```


```{r}
#| label: exploratory-rt
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Secondary effect reported in the original: staying with the previous choice, rare minus
# common (original Experiment 2: -3.62 +/- 0.89 %). Then the key difference by option type.
stay <- effect_summary(pe$stay_diff)
if (!is.null(stay)) {
  stay |>
    transmute(N, `Mean (points)` = round(estimate, 2), SEM = round(sem, 2),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high), p = fmt_p(p)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = sprintf(
      "Stay rate, rare minus common (original: %.2f +/- %.2f).", original_stay_mean, original_stay_sem))
}

by_type <- trials |>
  filter(task == "choice", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
  mutate(rare = as.logical(rare), chose_risky = as.numeric(chose_risky)) |>
  group_by(participant_id, option_type) |>
  summarise(diff = 100 * (mean(chose_risky[rare]) - mean(chose_risky[!rare])), .groups = "drop")
if (nrow(by_type) > 0) {
  by_type |>
    group_by(`Option type` = option_type) |>
    summarise(N = sum(!is.na(diff)), `Mean (points)` = round(mean(diff, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
              SEM = round(sd(diff, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(diff))), 2), .groups = "drop") |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Risky choices, rare minus common, by option type.")
}
```

## Discussion

### Summary of replication attempt

### Commentary


The exploratory analysis suggest that the participants who use replay (41 participants) have mean of +0.03 with SEM 1.81, while participants who don't use replay (79 participants) have mean of +3.23 with SEM 1.82. This may suggest that participants who need to use replay button show no effect to risky decision making after rare tone. This exploratory analysis result may have suggested the need for stricter sound check, i.e. dropping replay and restoring the 6 sequences sound checks. 


# Phase 2: Extension

**Track:**  Best-practices rescue

## Rationale


There are 3 possible reasons for Phase 1 did not reproduce the original result. First, we had too few sample for a smaller true effect. The effect estimated by our replication is +2.14 and this gives much lower than 80 % power with N=120. We can potentially address this issue by increasing sample size to N=200. 
Second, we had weaker sound check compare to the original paper. With 2 screens sound-check and replay option, guessers pass our 2-screen check around 11% of the time (compare to around 2% in the original paper). Another interesting observation from exploratory analysis suggest that participants who need to use replay button show no effect to risky decision making after rare tone (no replay users   +3.23 ± 1.82 and replay users: −0.03 ± 1.72 (n = 79 vs 43)). We can potentially address this issue by restoring the original 6 screens sound check (pass with 5 out of 6 correct) and removing the replay option.
The third reason is experiment fatigue, based on few participants feedback in the pilot and main study, the 17 minutes duration of the experiment might be too long. One of the possible changes to make is to cut the experiment duration to 10 minutes (i.e. with 60 trials instead of 120 trials per participant). However, the drawback is we would get less chance to observe the risky sound effect for each participants (15 trials instead of 30 trials), and we may need to double the sample size.



## Changes from Phase 1



| # | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Checks | 2-screen sound check with Replay, 2/2 to pass |  6-screen sound check, played once, 5/6 to pass | Participants from phase 1 who used replay show no effect, stricter sound check to screened out 'guesser' |
| 2 | Sample | N=120 | N=200 | The effect estimated by our replication is +2.14 and this gives much lower than 80 % power with N=120 |


Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.



## Power and sample



Considering the possible improvement through stricter sound check and no replay and based on the exploratory analysis of replay vs no-replay participants, we would expect the effect to move closer to original 4.03. Balancing the trade-off between effect size and budget constraints, we would power to 3 points instead of the phase 1 result of 2.14 or the original result of 4.03. To achieve at least 80% power at this effect size, we would require N=200 sample. Full analysis is presented in the table below.



```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
phase2_n <- 200   # planned analysed participants in Phase 2

p1_effect <- if (have_data) effect_summary(person_effects(phase1)$risk_diff)
basis_sd  <- if (!is.null(p1_effect)) p1_effect$estimate / p1_effect$dz else original_sd
basis_src <- if (!is.null(p1_effect)) "Phase 1" else "the original study"

half_width <- function(n) qt(0.975, n - 1) * basis_sd / sqrt(n)
power_at <- function(n, delta) {
  tryCatch(power.t.test(n = n, delta = delta, sd = basis_sd, sig.level = 0.05, type = "one.sample")$power,
           error = function(e) NA)
}
p1_est <- if (!is.null(p1_effect)) p1_effect$estimate else NA_real_
pct <- function(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1)

tibble(
  Study        = c(if (!is.null(p1_effect)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed` = c(if (!is.null(p1_effect)) p1_effect$N, phase2_n)
) |>
  mutate(`Power at 4.03 (original)`  = pct(map_dbl(`N analysed`, power_at, delta = original_mean)),
         `Power at 3`                = pct(map_dbl(`N analysed`, power_at, delta = 3)),
         `Power at Phase 1 estimate` = if (is.na(p1_est)) "" else pct(map_dbl(`N analysed`, power_at, delta = p1_est)),
         `95% CI half-width`         = sprintf("±%.2f points", map_dbl(`N analysed`, half_width))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf(
    "Power of the key test (one-sample t approximation, two-sided alpha = .05) and expected precision, using the SD of individual effects from %s (%.1f points)%s.",
    basis_src, basis_sd, if (is.na(p1_est)) "" else sprintf("; Phase 1 estimate = %.2f points", p1_est)))
```

## Analysis plan


For Phase 2 analysis, we will perform the same test as in Phase 1: Wilcoxon two-sided signed rank test on percentage difference of risky choice after rare and common tone for each participant. For exploratory analysis, we will report the pooled estimates across Phase 1 and Phase 2. We will also report the pooled estimate of participants in Phase 1 who did not use replay and Phase 2 participants, as this is a closer comparison to Phase 2 compare to considering every Phase 1 participants.

We will run Phase 2 under a new experiment id to avoid mixing the result with Phase 1.
